## CLAUDE
Got a real, complete round trip after finding and fixing three genuine bugs. Here's what happened:

**Three real bugs, found and fixed via actual runs against `21_08_2026` NATURALGAS data:**

1. **Zero fills (290 modifies, no trades)** — joining the crowd at the exact best bid meant re-pricing kept resetting FIFO queue priority faster than it could build. Fixed by price-improving the entry by one real tick (`ctx.refdata().get(instrument).tick_size`), putting the order alone at a fresh price level instead of at the back of an existing queue.
2. **`ctx.submit()` called from `on_fill`** — a `ControlHandler` callback where `can_submit=false` by design (fills are read-only notifications, orders only get placed from `on_book`/`on_trade`). This silently failed with `SubmitNotAllowedHere`, leaving the strategy stuck thinking it was still unfilled even though the entry had actually filled. Fixed with a one-tick transitional `Phase::EntryFilled` that defers the TP submission to the next `on_book`/`on_trade` call.
3. **TP price not on a valid tick** — `entry_price × 1.005` almost never lands on a tick boundary, so the venue denied it (`TICK_SIZE`). Fixed with a `round_up_to_tick` helper.

**One genuine market-microstructure finding, not a bug:** the exchange itself broadcasts a `MassDelete` right at session close (real MCX behavior, matching the existing `mass_delete_cancels_our_own_resting_order` test), wiping every resting order an instant before a force-close keyed to the exact same timestamp can win the race — the book is already empty by the time we try. Fixed by triggering the EOD force-close 5 minutes before the real session end instead of exactly at it.

**Final result**: entry BUY filled @ Rs 263.50 (10:00:05 IST, aggressive — the tick-improved bid crossed the spread), TP rested at Rs 264.90 all day unfilled, EOD force-close at 23:25 IST filled aggressively @ Rs 264.60 — net **+Rs 1,287.92** after costs. CRUDEOIL subscribed correctly but saw no book/trade events (its real data lives on a different capture stream than NATURALGAS's — the disclosed single-stream limitation from earlier this session).

Sent you the four output files: the full component-level event trail, order/fill logs, and P&L report. All 281 tests still pass.

## CLAUDE
Rewrote the strategy exactly as specified — strategy code only, nothing else touched. Rebuilt, all 281 tests still pass, and ran it against the real `21_08_2026` NATURALGAS data.

**What changed in the strategy:**
- Entry is now fully aggressive: `OrderType::MarketToLimit` BUY (no more resting limit, no more re-pricing/queue logic).
- No resting TP order either — position is monitored every tick against target/stop/timeout, and the exit itself is also `MarketToLimit`.
- Target = entry × 1.005 (0.5%), stop-loss = entry × 0.990 (1%).
- If neither fires within **176 seconds** of the entry fill, the position closes at market anyway (`TIMEOUT` reason).
- Continuous re-entry all session (5 min cooldown after each exit, then back in).
- Added retry handling in `on_order_update` for `Denied`/`Rejected` so a single failed order doesn't permanently freeze the instrument.

**Real result (13.5 real trading hours, `21_08_2026`):** 101 round trips, 202 fills, all same-side aggressive matches (`kind=Aggressive`). Every single exit was via **TIMEOUT** — the target (0.5%) and stop (1%) never got crossed within 176 seconds even once, which given NATURALGAS's real intraday tick-by-tick pace is a believable finding, not a bug: 0.5–1% moves in under 3 minutes are rare for this instrument. Net result was `-Rs 17,437` (gross `-8,625`, plus `~Rs 8,812` in accumulated costs across 202 fills) — expected for a strategy with no real edge, just noise plus transaction costs on every timeout-forced round trip.

Sent you the full trail: `events.log` (2,327 lines, every submit/fill/order-update/portfolio update), `orders.log` (404 transitions), `fills.log` (202 fills), `report.txt`.

## CLAUDE
`cost` in the report is **not** taxes alone — it's the full realistic MCX transaction-cost stack, computed per fill leg by `CostModel::round_trip` ([execution.rs:550](qtrade/src/execution/execution.rs#L550)):

| Component | Rate | Which side |
|---|---|---|
| Brokerage | flat **Rs 20/lot** | both |
| CTT (Commodity Transaction Tax) | 0.01% of turnover | **sell only** |
| Stamp duty | 0.002% of turnover | **buy only** |
| Exchange transaction charge | 0.00002% of turnover | both |
| SEBI turnover fee | 0.00001% of turnover | both |
| GST | 18% of (exchange charge + brokerage) | both |

`total_rupees` is just the sum of all six, applied identically pre-trade and post-trade so a strategy's own cost-aware quoting can never disagree with the real accounting.

**Why it added up to Rs 8,812 here:** this run had 202 fills (101 round trips × 2 legs). The two components that actually dominate:
- **Brokerage**: flat Rs 20 × 202 legs = **Rs 4,040** — this alone is nearly half the total, and it's a flat per-lot fee, not a tax, so it doesn't care how small the price move was.
- **CTT**: 0.01% of turnover, sell-side only, on ~101 sell legs at NATURALGAS's real turnover (price × lot size) — roughly **Rs 3,300**.

GST and stamp duty make up most of the rest (~Rs 1,400 combined); exchange/SEBI fees are negligible (a few rupees total).

So it's "this big" because the strategy round-tripped 101 times chasing 0.5%/1% moves that mostly never landed — each round trip pays a fixed Rs 40 brokerage regardless of outcome, plus CTT on the sell leg, so cost scales with **trade count**, not with how much money was actually made or lost on price. That's exactly why `net_pnl` (`-17,437`) came out so much worse than `gross_pnl` (`-8,625`): the cost model is charging for 202 real fills, not judging whether those fills were profitable.

One caveat, straight from the code's own comment: these rates are "placeholder, representative-of-MCX rates — not verified against a live rate circular." The mechanism (config-driven, direction-asymmetric) is real; the exact numbers haven't been checked against an actual current MCX/broker rate card.

## CLAUDE
You're right on the core insight, but let's get the count precise. In this codebase, `simulator::OrderType` ([simulator.rs:632](qtrade/src/simulator/simulator.rs#L632)) is the actual venue-facing order type — the only thing the exchange/SimExchange itself understands:

1. **`LimitDay(Price)`** — plain day limit, rests normally
2. **`BookOrCancel(Price)`** — post-only, rejected outright if it would cross
3. **`Ioc(Price)`** — immediate-or-cancel limit
4. **`MarketToLimit`** — sweeps available liquidity, residual rests as a limit at last traded price

So there are **4 real order types** defined, not 2. But you're right that our strategy currently only *uses* one of them: after the last rewrite, `multi_instrument_bracket` and `naturalgas_bracket` both submit **`MarketToLimit` exclusively** — for the entry, the TP exit, the SL exit, and the EOD exit alike. The only thing that varies is `Side` (Buy/Sell), which isn't an order type at all, just direction. If "2 types" is what you're counting, it's probably entry-vs-exit as a workflow distinction — but at the wire level those are the identical `OrderType` variant.

Your real point stands, though, and it's correct: **there is no "target order" or "bracket order" as a venue-recognized type anywhere in this system.** `SimExchange`/`OrderType` has no concept of an order that natively carries a target + stop-loss. What the strategy calls "TP"/"SL" is pure strategy-side logic — `tick_state` reads `ctx.book(instrument).best_bid()` on every tick and independently fires a brand-new, plain `MarketToLimit` sell the instant a threshold crosses. The exchange never sees "this is my target price" — it only ever sees a fresh, ordinary sell order arrive at whatever moment we decided to submit it.

This actually mirrors real MCX/CTCL reality: the exchange itself only speaks a handful of raw order types (limit, market, SL, SL-M, plus IOC/GTC time-in-force flags) — a genuine "bracket order" or "cover order" with a built-in target+stoploss (the kind retail brokers like Zerodha offer) is a **broker-side OMS construct**, not an exchange primitive. The broker's software does exactly what our strategy does: place the entry, watch the market, and fire off separate plain orders for the target/stop-loss legs. So the design here isn't a shortcut — it's structurally how real bracket orders work under the hood.

One gotcha if you grep it yourself: the file trips `grep`'s binary-content heuristic somewhere, so plain `grep` returns nothing silently — you need `grep -a`.

## What MCX ETI actually recognizes

Three **orthogonal** dimensions, not one flat list:

**OrdType (tag 40)** — the order type itself:
| Value | Type | Behavior |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | Limit | Won't execute worse than the limit price |
| 3 | Stop Market | Hidden from the book until trigger price is crossed, then becomes a Market order |
| 4 | Stop Limit | Same trigger mechanism, converts to a Limit order instead |
| 5 | Market To Limit | Sweeps available liquidity; unfilled residual **rests as a Limit** at the last traded price (doesn't vanish) |
| 6 / 7 | Auction Buy In / Sell Out | Special auction-session types, not continuous trading |

**TimeInForce (tag 59)**, independent of OrdType: Day(0), GTC(1, Standard orders only), IOC(3), GTD(6, Standard only), Session/EOS(7).

**ExecInst (tag 18)**, also independent: Persistent vs Non-Persistent ("Lean"), plus a documented "Book or Cancel" behavior (`ExecRestatementReason=212` on execution reports) — post-only, rejected rather than resting if it would cross.

## This project already answered your exact question

Before any code existed, **`ARCHITECTURE-DECISIONS.md` D12 ("Order types in scope")** recorded this same taxonomy and drew a deliberate phase-1 line:

- **In scope**: Limit-Day, Book-or-Cancel, IOC, Market-to-Limit — this is *exactly* `simulator::OrderType`'s 4 current variants, already matching MCX's real semantics (D12 literally cites `OrdType=2`/`5` the same way I just found in the spec).
- **Out of scope, "recorded as a decision not an oversight"**: Stop Market, Stop Limit, Auction Buy In/Sell Out, iceberg.

So the gap you noticed last message — no native "target order," we monitor the book and fire a plain order ourselves — isn't a bug or an oversight. It's D12 talking: MCX genuinely offers native Stop Market/Stop Limit order types (server-side, hidden-until-triggered, exactly what a "bracket" would need), and this project deliberately chose not to model them in phase 1. It's a real, currently-parked capability, not something we'd be inventing from scratch if you wanted it later.

One more decided-but-not-built gap while I was in there: **D13** says the order model should carry an explicit Standard/Lean (persistent/non-persistent) attribute "from day one" — it isn't actually on `NewOrderRequest` today. Separate from your question, flagging it since it's the same kind of decided-vs-implemented gap.

## Your adapter-layer instinct — already named and placed

`ARCHITECTURE.md` already commits to exactly this, before either of us touched it:

```
LAYER 3 — CORE (exchange- and mode-agnostic): ExecutionEngine, Order Validation, Strategies...
                ↓ order commands           ↑ execution reports
VENUE EDGE (per mode): Simulated Exchange  |  Exchange Gateway
```

§4.12: *"[ExecutionEngine] cannot tell the Simulated Exchange from the Exchange Gateway. Both present the same interface: commands in, reports out."* — the canonical vocabulary `ExecutionEngine`/`Ctx`/strategies speak is `simulator::OrderType`/`NewOrderRequest`/`ExecReport`, **not** raw MCX wire tags. `SimExchange` today plays the MCX-backtest-gateway role directly, implementing D12's real MCX matching rules but never touching an actual wire byte. A real live "Exchange Gateway" (§3.2 table, Stage 11 in the build order, not yet built) would sit at that same edge and translate the identical canonical types into real ETI messages (New Order Single-10100, Replace-10106, Cancel-10109, Execution Report-10103, etc.) and back.

NSE is explicitly deferred (§1.3) at the same edge — its own future Exchange Gateway, same interface. And the Normalizer's stated rule for the feed side (D32: *"if a decoder cannot express something in the internal vocabulary, the vocabulary is wrong — widening it with optional fields is not the fix"*) is the right rule to carry over to the order side too: if NSE has a genuine order concept our 4-variant `OrderType` can't express, we widen the canonical enum for everyone, not bolt an NSE-only flag onto it.

**My opinion, concretely:**
1. Don't build a new abstraction — the seam already exists and MCX already fits it perfectly (D12 ⇄ `simulator::OrderType` line up exactly).
2. The real next piece, whenever you want it, is the actual **MCX Exchange Gateway** (wire encode/decode against this same `mcx_eti.txt` spec), sitting behind `ExecutionEngine` exactly where `SimExchange` sits today — not a redesign, just the second implementation of an interface that's already been proven by the backtest side.
3. NSE stays parked until you decide to open it — at which point it's a new Gateway behind the same interface, and `OrderType` only grows if NSE has something MCX genuinely doesn't (its own Stop-Loss/SL-M naming, disclosed-quantity rules, etc. — worth its own real spec read when that day comes, same as we just did for MCX).
4. Reopening D12 to add Stop Market/Stop Limit natively is a separate, legitimate call — real MCX capability, currently fenced off on purpose — worth deciding on its own merits, not as a side effect of the adapter discussion.

Where do you want to take this next — reopen D12 for native stop orders, or start sketching the real MCX Exchange Gateway against this spec?

Quincy is a market-data redistribution company — they connect to CME (and a bunch of other exchanges) themselves, translate the raw exchange protocol into their own normalized binary format, and this firm subscribes to *Quincy's* feed rather than speaking CME's native MDP3.0/SBE protocol directly. This exact choice is already recorded in your own `ARCHITECTURE.md`: `CME | Price signal | MBP | 5 levels | Quincy QED`. This file is essentially the historical source that line was written from.

**Where the recorded data comes from:** a plain local file (`fopen(file, "r")` in `Add_ReplayFile`), not a live socket. It's a recording of exactly what Quincy's own "Distribution Server" sent, captured earlier by this firm's own capture tooling. The live path (commented out — `QEDC_init_context`/multicast setup isn't shown here) would instead be a UDP multicast subscription to Quincy directly.

**The recorded file's own framing** (`Start_FileReplay`, lines 468-470):
```
timestamp = (int64_t*)(Buffer + Processed_Bytes)          // 8 bytes: capture timestamp
MSG_LEN   = *(int32_t*)(Buffer + Processed_Bytes + 8)     // 4 bytes: payload length
                                                            // then MSG_LEN bytes: the raw Quincy packet
```
Same idea as MCX's own capture files you've already reverse-engineered this session (an outer length+timestamp wrapper around each real payload) — just a different byte layout, because it's the same firm's capture tool wrapping a different vendor's wire format.

**What's inside that payload:** a Quincy "packet," which can be **encrypted** (`QEDC_is_encrypted_packet`/`QEDC_decrypt_packet`, keyed by a file this firm holds) and can bundle **multiple messages**. `QED_parser_begin`/`QED_parser_next` (lines 328, 421) iterate through them one at a time.

**What each decoded message looks like:** a `QED_msg` — Quincy's own normalized record, not CME-specific. It carries the instrument's symbol ("topic"), *three* timestamps (`src_time` = exchange time, `ds_rcv_time`/`ds_snd_time` = when Quincy's own server received/forwarded it — richer than MCX's two, since it separates "exchange → Quincy" latency from "Quincy → us" latency), and on a normal update, a **top-5-levels-per-side snapshot** (price + qty + order count, both sides) plus any trade prints. That confirms CME here is delivered as a maintained MBP-5 book, not raw order-by-order MBO like MCX — exactly what your venue table already says.

**What the code does with it** (the `generate_feed` loop, lines 345-418): looks up the instrument by symbol in a pre-built map (filtered to the CME segment out of a larger shared contract list — the same kind of instrument filter qtrade does), refreshes a per-instrument running struct with those 5 levels + last trade, and — only once both sides of the book actually exist and aren't crossed (`SellPrice[0] > BuyPrice[0]`) — packages it into a common `Token_Data` struct and calls `feed_func(Segment, &fdata)`.

## CLAUDE
Let me back up and explain this like you're seeing a market-data feed for the first time — no jargon without unpacking it first.

## The big picture first

Every second, an exchange (like CME) is shouting out updates: "Natural Gas futures — best buyer wants to pay $2.501, best seller wants $2.502" and "a trade just happened at $2.501." A trading firm needs to *listen* to that shouting, understand it, and feed it into their strategy code. That's all this file does — it's a listener + translator. Nothing more mysterious than that.

## 1. What's a "stream" here, and how does data flow?

Think of a **stream** as one continuous radio channel of updates for one thing — e.g., "all updates for the Natural Gas contract." A firm might record several such channels at once (one per contract, or one per group of contracts), and each recorded channel is saved as its own file.

The flow, step by step:
```
Exchange (CME) → Quincy (a middleman company) → recorded to a file → this code reads the file → decodes each update → hands it to the rest of the trading system
```

So "data flow" just means: bytes move from a file, through a few translation steps, into a normal, C++ struct the rest of the program can actually read (prices, quantities, etc.) instead of raw 1s and 0s.

## 2. Where does the recorded file come from, and how does it get read/decoded?

**Where it comes from:** Nobody in this code creates the file — it's a *recording*, made earlier, of real messages that arrived over the network on some past trading day. Think of it like a voicemail recording: someone already "listened" once, live, and saved every message to disk. `Start_FileReplay` doesn't listen live — it just re-plays that saved recording, like playing back the voicemail.

**Who made the recording, and in what format?** Here's the twist: this firm doesn't talk to CME directly. They pay a company called **Quincy Data** to do that for them. Quincy connects to CME (and many other exchanges), and translates CME's own complicated format into Quincy's *own* simpler, standard format. So what got recorded to this file isn't "raw CME data" — it's "Quincy's translated version of CME data." This code then only needs to know how to read Quincy's format (using Quincy's own toolkit, the `QED_*` functions), not CME's.

**How it's read, concretely** — opening the file is like opening a book that's structured as a repeating pattern:
```
[timestamp][how many bytes come next][ ... that many bytes of actual message data ... ]
[timestamp][how many bytes come next][ ... that many bytes of actual message data ... ]
[timestamp][how many bytes come next][ ... that many bytes of actual message data ... ]
   ... repeats until end of file ...
```
The code reads the timestamp and length first (so it knows exactly how many more bytes to grab), then reads that chunk, and hands that chunk to Quincy's decoder (`QED_parser_begin`), which turns those raw bytes into something readable: "this is symbol X, best bid is $2.501 for 5 lots, best ask is $2.502 for 3 lots," etc.

That readable result is called a `QED_msg` in this code — think of it as "the translated, human-readable version of one update."

## 3. "One shared normalized-event vocabulary across MCX, CME, and DGCX" — what did I mean?

Here's the problem: MCX, CME, and DGCX are three *completely different* exchanges, each with their own unique message formats — different byte layouts, different field names, different units. If the rest of the trading program had to understand all three formats directly, every single piece of code downstream (the strategy, the order book, the risk checks) would need special-case logic for "if this came from MCX do X, if from CME do Y, if from DGCX do Z." That would be a nightmare to maintain.

The fix — and what "shared vocabulary" means — is: no matter which exchange a message came from, translate it into **one common struct** that always looks the same. In this old C++ code, that common struct is called `Token_Data`. It always has the same fields (instrument ID, timestamp, best prices/quantities, last trade, etc.) regardless of whether the original message came from MCX's feeder file or CME's feeder file.

So `MCX_Feeder.cpp` and `CME_Feeder.cpp` are two *different* translators (because the incoming raw formats are different), but both translators produce the *exact same kind of output* (`Token_Data`) at the end. That's the "shared vocabulary" — like two different foreign-language interpreters who both translate into the same target language (English), so the person listening doesn't need to know which original language was spoken.

This matters for you because **your `qtrade` project already follows this exact same idea** — it's just called something else there. Your `ARCHITECTURE.md` calls this the "Normalizer," and the common struct in your project's design is meant to be your own internal event type (not tied to MCX specifically), so that if you ever add a second exchange, the rest of `qtrade`'s code (book building, strategies, execution) never needs to change or know which exchange the data came from.

## 4. The replay loop — what's actually happening?

Forget the code for a second. Imagine you have **three separate voicemail recordings** — one for Natural Gas, one for Crude Oil, one for USD/INR — and each recording has its own timestamps. You want to listen to all three recordings **interleaved, in the correct real-world order they originally happened**, not "finish recording 1, then recording 2, then recording 3."

So the logic is:
1. Peek at the very next message in *each* recording (without processing it yet) — just check its timestamp.
2. Whichever recording has the **earliest** next timestamp — process that one message from that recording.
3. Go back to step 1 and repeat, forever, until every recording has run out.

That's the entire replay loop. It's just: *"always play whichever recording's next message happened earliest, across all the recordings you have open."* This guarantees that when you replay multiple instruments/streams together, events come out in the same chronological order they actually occurred in real life — which matters enormously for backtesting, because a strategy trading two instruments needs to see "Crude Oil ticked up" before "Natural Gas ticked down" if that's genuinely the order it happened in reality.

The rest of the code in that loop (`Processed_Bytes`, `Pos`, `BytesToRead`, `MSG_LEN`) is just bookkeeping for "how much of the file have I already read, and how many more bytes do I need before I have a complete message" — the kind of low-level plumbing you'd need whenever you're reading a file in chunks rather than all at once. Don't worry about memorizing those variable names; the *idea* (peek timestamps, always advance the earliest one) is the only part that matters conceptually.

---

Does this land better? Happy to walk through one concrete tiny example (like: 3 fake messages with timestamps, tracing exactly which one gets processed first, second, third) if that would make the replay-loop idea more concrete.

## CLAUDE
Found the definitive answer, straight from Quincy's own header file — no guessing needed. **`qed_msg.h`, line 157-159:**

> *"Return the number of visible price levels in the book... **QED sends fixed depth snapshots for all instruments.**"*

So: **CME (via Quincy) is snapshot-style, not MBO.** This is a real, structural difference from MCX, and it explains a lot about why the code looks the way it does.

## MBO vs. snapshot — in plain terms

**MCX (what you already know, MBO = "Market By Order"):** the exchange tells you about *individual orders*. Something like: *"Order #55512 was just added: 5,000 qty at price 263.40."* Later: *"Order #55512 was just deleted."* The exchange never tells you "here's the book" — it only tells you the individual events, and **you** (the receiving program) have to add/remove those orders yourself, one at a time, to build up what the book currently looks like. This is why `qtrade`'s `book.rs` is genuinely complex — it has to track every individual resting order, its queue position, etc.

**CME via Quincy (snapshot-style, sometimes called MBP = "Market By Price"):** nobody tells you about individual orders at all. Instead, every time something changes, you just get handed the **current picture directly**: *"Right now: level 0 bid = 2.501 for 5,000 qty (3 orders resting there), level 1 bid = 2.500 for 2,000 qty (1 order)..."* all the way down a fixed number of levels (5, per your `ARCHITECTURE.md`). You never have to reconstruct anything yourself — Quincy has already done the work of turning "a pile of individual orders" into "here's the top 5 prices and total size at each" before it ever reaches this code.

That "number of orders" field you saw (`QED_msg_level_number_of_orders`) is just a **count** — "3 orders are sitting at this price" — never their individual identities. You can't tell *which* 3 orders they are, or track one specific order's position in the queue the way you can with MCX's MBO feed. The header even says this count is only given for the top 2 levels, not all 5.

## Why this matters practically

This is exactly why the CME code you read doesn't have anything resembling `book.rs`'s order-tracking logic. Look back at what `CONTRACT_DETAILS` stores: just plain arrays — `BuyPrice[5]`, `BuyQty[5]`, `NoOfBuyOrds[5]`, and so on. There's no "order list," no "queue," no individual order IDs being tracked anywhere in this file. There's nothing to reconstruct — each incoming `QED_msg` just **overwrites** those arrays with whatever the new snapshot says, and that's the whole "book building" step for CME. Compare that to how much more machinery MCX needs.

One more precise detail worth knowing: "fixed depth snapshot" means each update message repeats the **entire** top-5 picture again, not just "level 2 changed, here's the new level 2." That's also why the code checks a `QED_BOOK_UNCHANGED` flag first (line 162 in the .cpp) — to skip re-processing a message where the snapshot happens to be identical to last time.

**Bottom line for your original question:** you can't get MBO-level detail (individual order tracking, queue position, priority) out of this CME feed even if you wanted to — Quincy simply doesn't send it. What you get is a clean, already-aggregated top-of-book snapshot, which is easier to consume but structurally less detailed than what you have for MCX.

## CLAUDE
You're right, and here's the precise reason why — grounded in your actual `Book` trait, not just the general MBO/MBP distinction.

## Your `Book` trait is already MBP-shaped

Look at `qtrade/src/book/book.rs`, line 39:
```rust
pub trait Book {
    fn best_bid(&self) -> Option<PriceLevel>;
    fn best_ask(&self) -> Option<PriceLevel>;
    fn depth(&self, n: usize) -> Vec<PriceLevel>;   // top n levels, both sides
    fn qty_at_price(&self, side: Side, price: Price) -> Qty;
    fn state(&self) -> BookState;
}
```
This is exactly "give me the current price + quantity per level" — nothing about individual orders. This is what every strategy actually sees when it calls `ctx.book(instrument)`, regardless of the venue.

Then there's a **separate, extra** trait, `MboBook` (line 55):
```rust
pub trait MboBook: Book {
    fn queue_position(&self, handle: OrderHandle) -> Option<i64>;
}
```
`queue_position` — "how much quantity is resting ahead of my order in the queue" — is the one capability that genuinely *needs* individual-order tracking, because you can only answer "who's ahead of me" if you know each individual order's arrival priority. This extra trait is bolted on top of `Book`, not baked into it — a deliberate separation.

**So: `MboBookImpl`/`BookBuilder`/`OrderSlot` (the whole incremental order-tracking machinery) exists *only* to satisfy `MboBook`'s extra `queue_position` requirement.** If you never need `queue_position` for an instrument, you never need that machinery — you just need something that implements the plain `Book` trait.

## Why CME never needs `queue_position` at all

Two independent reasons stack up here:
1. **Quincy's feed structurally can't support it** — it only gives you a count of orders per level, never their identities or arrival order (confirmed last message).
2. **Your own `ARCHITECTURE.md` never intends to trade on CME anyway** — its stated role is `"Price signal"`, read-only reference pricing to inform your MCX quotes, not a venue you submit orders to. You'd never ask "where's my order in CME's queue" because you'd never have an order resting on CME in the first place.

So a CME book implementation would only ever need to satisfy plain `Book` — and since Quincy already hands you the top-5-levels-per-side snapshot directly, that implementation is just: *"store whatever the last snapshot said, return it when asked."* No incremental add/modify/delete logic, no `OrderSlot`, no priority timestamps — just a small holder struct that copies Quincy's 5 levels in and reads them back out.

## One honest caveat: this doesn't exist yet

## The two files disagree about what's actually IN the capture files

**`CME_Feeder.cpp` (the old one):** reads each record as `[8B timestamp][4B length][length bytes of raw Quincy-encoded data]`, then calls `QED_parser_begin`/`QED_parser_next` — the real Quincy SDK — to decode those bytes into a `QED_msg`. **My read on which one is right, based on real evidence, not a guess:** Look at `CME_Feeder.h`'s own `CONTRACT_DETAILS` struct (`BuyPrice[5]`, `BuyQty[5]`, `SellPrice[5]`, `SellQty[5]`, `NoOfBuyOrds[5]`, `NoOfSellOrds[5]`, `LastTradedPrice`, bitfields, `GenericContract Contract`) — it's **the exact same shape** as the struct `CME_parsefeed.cpp` reads directly off disk. That's the tell: the real recorder (`CME_Recorder`, the ELF binary sitting at `/mnt/CME_Recording_Files/`) almost certainly does the live Quincy decoding itself, in memory, the way `CME_Feeder.cpp`'s logic shows — and then **writes the already-populated `CONTRACT_DETAILS` struct to disk**, not the raw Quincy bytes. `CME_parsefeed.cpp` is reading exactly that output. `CME_Feeder.cpp` looks like it documents an earlier/different stage of this pipeline (or a different capture mode) that isn't what's actually sitting in `/mnt/CME_Recording_Files/` today.

Also worth noting: the new framing (`[8B length][8B timestamp]`, length first) matches the pattern MCX's own capture files use — the old framing (`[8B timestamp][4B length]`, timestamp first) doesn't. That's a second, independent signal pointing the same direction.

**Bottom line: if this holds, decoding real CME data is dramatically simpler than we thought last time — no Quincy protocol work needed at all, just reading a fixed, documented struct.** But this is inference from evidence, not something I've confirmed byte-for-byte against a real file yet — flagging that honestly rather than asserting it.

## Now, the expiry issue — I think I found exactly what you're sensing

The PDF says (§4, offset `0x09`): **`ExpiryDate int32_t` — "Expiration date integer representation (YYYYMMDD)"**. So CME's expiry is a plain decimal calendar date, like `20260919`.

I checked how your **existing MCX code** handles the same-sounding field. `refdata.rs`, line 33-37:
```rust
/// MCX's contract file stamps `ExpiryDate` (`parts[54]`) as a Unix-epoch
/// second count that is off by the IST offset -- see refdata_user_doc.md
/// for how this was verified against real rows.
const IST_OFFSET_SECONDS: i64 = 19_800; // 5 hours 30 minutes
```
MCX's `ExpiryDate` is a **Unix-epoch seconds count**, minus an IST offset, then divided by seconds-per-day to get a day number. That's a completely different encoding from "plain YYYYMMDD integer."

**This is the real danger:** if anyone builds the CME decoder by pattern-matching MCX's approach — "oh, `ExpiryDate` is an int32, same field name, must be the same kind of value" — and reuses that epoch-seconds-minus-IST-offset formula on CME's `ExpiryDate`, the result would be nonsense. Feeding `20260919` through "treat as epoch seconds, divide by 86400" gives you a date in **1970**, not 2026 — the two encodings are not interchangeable at all, even though both fields are `int32_t` and named the same thing.

## One honest caveat before trusting either document

The PDF has some hallmarks of being a reconstructed/generated spec rather than an original vendor document — compare its generic "Validated Specification" / "Key Integration Notes" styling against the genuine Quincy headers we read earlier (real copyright notices, real terse vendor doc-comment style). Yes — exactly that. Let me say it as simply as possible.

## The core point, in one sentence

The old file (`CME_Feeder.cpp`) expects to receive **raw, scrambled data** that it has to translate itself (using Quincy's toolkit). The new file (`CME_parsefeed.cpp`) expects to receive data that's **already translated** — it just reads it straight, no translation step needed.

## A simple analogy

Think of it like a letter written in French.

- **Old file's approach:** "Here's a letter written in French. Let me use my French dictionary/translator to figure out what it says, sentence by sentence."
- **New file's approach:** "Someone already translated this letter into English for me. I can just read it directly — no dictionary needed."

Both files are reading "a recorded file," but they disagree about **what language that file is written in**. And based on what I found (the new file's data shape matches exactly what the old file's translator *produces* after it finishes translating), my best guess is: **the real files sitting on your machine are already-translated (English), and the new file (`CME_parsefeed.cpp`) is the correct way to read them.** The old file was maybe describing an earlier step in the process — the "translating" step itself — not the final file you actually have.

So: good news if that's true — building this decoder is simpler than we first thought, since there's no "translating" work needed at all, just reading a fixed, well-labeled layout directly.

## And the expiry-date worry, in plain terms

Think of "expiry date" as just answering: "when does this contract expire?"

- **MCX stores it** as a big weird number that means "seconds since Jan 1, 1970" (like a stopwatch that's been running since 1970) — you have to do math on that number to turn it into an actual date.
- **CME (per the new document) stores it** as a plain, human-readable number that just *looks like* the date itself — e.g., `20260919` literally means "2026, September, 19th." No stopwatch math needed at all.

These are two totally different ways of writing down "a date" in a computer. If someone building the CME decoder copies the MCX "stopwatch math" approach because it worked for MCX, it will produce a **garbage, wrong date** for CME — because CME isn't using stopwatch-style numbers at all, it's using plain readable numbers.

That mismatch — using MCX's math on CME's numbers — is exactly the kind of bug you were sensing. I haven't 100% proven yet that CME really works the "plain readable number" way (the document says so, but documents can be wrong) — I'd want to check one real file to be sure before we build anything around that assumption.

You caught something real, and I should be precise about it: **I didn't discard a second timestamp — there genuinely isn't one in this struct.** But your broader instinct (that something's missing) is correct, and I can show you exactly where.

## `RcTime` is almost certainly the local receive time, not the exchange time

The field is literally named `RcTime` — "Rc" = **R**e**c**eive. It sits *outside* `CONTRACT_DETAILS` entirely, in the outer file framing (`[8B length][8B RcTime][CONTRACT_DETAILS]`) — the exact same position and role as MCX's own "local capture timestamp" wrapper we found earlier this session. So yes: this is "when the recording machine got it," not "when the exchange sent it."

## I checked the actual struct fields — there's no second timestamp anywhere

`CONTRACT_DETAILS` and its embedded `GenericContract` (both straight from `CME_parsefeed.cpp`, confirmed byte-for-byte via real compilation) have exactly: 5 levels of buy/sell price+qty+order-count, last trade fields, and the contract metadata (symbol, expiry, tick size, etc.). No exchange timestamp field exists in either struct. So there was nothing for me to "decode and discard" — the PDF didn't hide anything from us; the struct itself was never designed to carry one.

## But here's the concrete evidence that the exchange timestamp *does* exist upstream, and was deliberately left out

Open `CME_Feeder.cpp` (which you have up) and look at `generate_feed()`. Quincy's real `QED_msg` object carries **three** timestamps, not one — confirmed by the `printMsg()` diagnostic function earlier in that same file:
```cpp
uint64_t srcTime = QED_msg_get_src_time(msg);      // exchange/market time
uint64_t dsRcvTime = QED_msg_get_ds_rcv_time(msg);  // Quincy's own receive time
uint64_t dsSendTime = QED_msg_get_ds_snd_time(msg); // Quincy's own send time
```
But in `generate_feed()` — the function that actually builds the real output record — both branches do this instead:
```cpp
fdata.Timestamp = *timestamp;   // the OUTER local capture time, passed in as a parameter
```
`QED_msg_get_src_time()` is never called there. The original developer clearly *knew* about the exchange timestamp (they used it in the debug-print function a few dozen lines earlier) but chose not to carry it into the actual per-tick record that gets saved.

## So, plainly

This isn't something the PDF hid, or something I dropped — it's a real, pre-existing choice baked into the original C++ pipeline, before either of us touched it. This capture format only ever kept "when we received it," and the exchange's own timestamp for each individual quote update was discarded upstream, before the file we're reading was even written. If exact exchange-side timing ever matters for this data, this particular capture format can't give it to you — that would need going back to a stage of the pipeline that still has access to Quincy's raw `QED_msg`, which this flattened format no longer carries.

## CLAUDE
Here's `naturalgas_bracket` in plain trading terms — no code, just what it actually does as a strategy.

## The core idea: a "bracket" trade

A "bracket" means: buy something, then immediately protect that position with two exit orders — a stop-loss (sell if it drops too far, cap the loss) and a take-profit (sell if it rises enough, lock in the gain). Whichever one gets hit first closes the trade. That's the whole shape of this strategy, repeated all day.

## Walking through one full cycle

1. **Wait for 10:00 AM IST.** Before that, the strategy does nothing at all — it just watches the market go by.

2. **At 10:00 AM, buy 1 lot of Natural Gas**, at whatever price is available right now (a "market" order — take the current price, don't haggle over an exact number). It then waits to actually see the fill confirmation come back.

3. **Once bought, watch the price on every tick.** Say it bought at ₹263.50. It continuously checks:
   - Has the price fallen to 99.5% of that (₹262.28)? → **Stop-loss** — sell now, cut the loss.
   - Has the price risen to 100.5% of that (₹264.83)? → **Take-profit** — sell now, take the gain.
   - Neither yet? → keep waiting, check again next tick.

4. **Whichever one triggers first, sell immediately** (again, at market price — take whatever's available). That closes the "round trip": one buy, one sell, done.

5. **Wait 5 minutes**, then go back to step 2 and do it all again — buy another lot, bracket it the same way, repeat for the rest of the trading day.

6. **At 11:30 PM IST (end of day), force-close anything still open** — if it's mid-trade when the session's about to end, it sells immediately rather than carrying the position overnight.

So over a full session, this strategy might complete many small round trips — buy, get stopped out or take profit, cool down 5 minutes, buy again — not just one trade.

## Why ±0.5%, specifically

The file's own comments explain this was tuned from a real test: it originally tried ±2% (buy, then wait for a 2% move either way), and on a real trading day that band **never triggered even once** — Natural Gas just didn't move 2% away from the 10 AM price all session. So it was tightened to ±0.5%, which is still a deliberate, real threshold (not noise-chasing every tiny wiggle), but close enough that it actually produces visible trades to observe.

## Two honest limitations worth knowing about

1. **The stop-loss/take-profit aren't real resting orders sitting at the exchange** — MCX doesn't offer a native "stop" order type in this system yet (we discussed this a few days ago — it's a deliberately parked feature, not an oversight). So instead, the strategy is *watching the price itself* every tick and manually firing a sell the instant a threshold is crossed. It's reactive, one tick behind the actual crossing — not a standing order that fires itself.

2. **No retry if an order gets rejected.** If a buy or sell somehow gets denied (by a risk check) or rejected (by the exchange), this strategy just sits there waiting forever for a fill that's never coming. It's not built to recover from that — acceptable for a first version, but a real strategy should handle it.

## The "state machine" shape

Under the hood, the strategy is always in exactly one of six "phases" (waiting to enter, waiting for the buy to fill, holding the position, waiting for the sell to fill, cooling down, or done for the day) and each tick just asks "given where I am right now, does anything need to happen?" That's a common, clean way to structure this kind of always-on, all-day trading logic — worth keeping in mind as a pattern for whatever MCX strategy comes next.

Ready to move into planning new MCX strategies whenever you are.

## CLAUDE
Good catch to think through — but the premise doesn't quite match how the code actually behaves. Let me correct that first, then answer the real question.

## What actually happens if price never moves

The 5-minute cooldown **doesn't start on its own** — it only starts *after* a position closes (via stop-loss, take-profit, or end-of-day). Look at the code: `CoolingDown` is only entered inside `on_fill`, when an exit fill comes in. There's no independent "check every 5 minutes regardless" timer.

So if the price genuinely never moves at all after the 10:00 AM entry — never touches ₹262.28 (stop-loss) or ₹264.83 (take-profit) — the strategy just **stays in the `Open` phase, holding that one position, all day.** It never gets a second entry, because it never got a chance to exit and re-enter. There's no "buy another one after 5 minutes" in that scenario — there's exactly one trade, held for the whole session.

## What actually closes it

The only thing that would end it is the end-of-day force-close at 11:30 PM — the strategy sells at whatever price is available then. If the price truly never moved, that's still ₹263.50 — the exact same price it bought at.

## Now, profit or loss?

**On price alone: exactly zero.** Bought at ₹263.50, sold at ₹263.50 — no gain, no loss from price movement.

**But real costs still apply regardless of price movement**, and they're not zero. We worked through this exact cost model a few days ago — brokerage is a flat per-lot fee, CTT is a tax on the sell leg, stamp duty on the buy leg, plus GST and exchange charges, all charged whether the trade made money or not. Using the real numbers from this exact scenario (this is the same entry price, ₹263.50, from an actual run we did earlier):

- Buy leg cost: ≈ **Rs 30.30**
- Sell leg cost: ≈ **Rs 56.79**
- **Total: ≈ Rs 87 lost**, purely from fees — even though the price never moved a single paisa.

So the honest answer is: **a small, guaranteed loss (~Rs 87 for 1 lot), not a breakeven.** This is actually a real, useful thing to keep in mind for any strategy — every round trip has a fixed cost floor it has to clear before it's even breakeven, regardless of whether the price prediction was right.

## CLAUDE
## Order types MCX ETI actually defines

Per the real circular (§4.4 "Order Types," plus the message-level `OrdType` (tag 40) table), there are **6 order types**, on top of two independent modifier dimensions:

**OrdType (tag 40) — the order type itself:**
| Value | Type | Behavior |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | Limit | Won't execute worse than the limit price |
| 3 | Stop Market | Hidden until a trigger price is crossed, then becomes a Market order |
| 4 | Stop Limit | Same trigger mechanism, becomes a Limit order instead |
| 5 | Market To Limit | Sweeps available liquidity; unfilled residual rests as a Limit at the last traded price |
| 6 | Auction Buy In | Special auction-session order, not continuous trading |
| 7 | Auction Sell Out | Same, sell side |

**TimeInForce (tag 59)**, independent of OrdType: Day, GTC (Standard orders only), IOC, GTD (Standard only), Session/EOS.

**ExecInst (tag 18)**, also independent: Persistent vs. Non-Persistent ("Lean"), plus a documented "Book or Cancel" (post-only) behavior.

## Are we mapping these in the backtester?

**Only 4 of the 6, and it's a deliberate, already-recorded decision — not an oversight.** `simulator::OrderType` today has exactly:

```rust
LimitDay(Price)      // OrdType=2, TIF=Day
BookOrCancel(Price)  // post-only
Ioc(Price)           // OrdType=2, TIF=IOC
MarketToLimit        // OrdType=5
```

This matches `ARCHITECTURE-DECISIONS.md` **D12 ("Order types in scope")** exactly, which explicitly lists these 4 as in-scope for phase 1, and separately states:

> *"Out of scope, recorded as a decision not an oversight: Stop Market (3), Stop Limit (4), Auction Buy In / Sell Out (6/7), iceberg."*

So **Stop Market and Stop Limit — the two order types that would let a strategy set a real, exchange-side stop-loss/target instead of watching the book and reacting a tick late (exactly what `naturalgas_bracket` has to do today) — are the two genuinely missing, real MCX capabilities.** Auction Buy In/Sell Out are missing too, but those only matter during the opening/closing auction, which this project doesn't model trading during anyway.

One more gap, separate from D12: **the Persistent/Non-Persistent ("Lean") distinction isn't implemented at all** — `NewOrderRequest` has no such field, even though D13 says the order model should carry it "from day one." Worth keeping in mind, but it's a different kind of gap (decided-but-never-built, not deliberately-parked).

## CLAUDE
Let's use a simple shopping analogy throughout — you're trying to buy or sell something at a certain price, and each order type is just a different **instruction** for how to do that.

## The 4 order types MCX offers

**1. Limit order** — "Buy it, but only at this price or better, and never worse."
> Example: Natural Gas is trading around ₹263.50. You place a Limit Buy at ₹263.00. It sits and waits. It only fills if the price actually comes down to ₹263.00 or lower. If the market never drops that far, your order just sits there unfilled, forever (or until you cancel it).

**2. Market To Limit** — "Buy it right now, at whatever price is available."
> Example: You want Natural Gas *now*, no haggling. You place a Market To Limit Buy. It grabs whatever is available at the best price the second it arrives — say it fills 1 lot at ₹263.55. If there wasn't enough available to fill your whole order immediately, whatever's left over automatically turns into a *resting Limit order* at that last price, rather than just disappearing or chasing the price further.

**3. Stop Market** — "Don't do anything yet — but the moment the price crosses this trigger, immediately buy/sell at whatever price is available."
> Example: You own Natural Gas bought at ₹263.50, and you want to automatically get out if it falls to ₹262.00 (protecting yourself from a bigger loss). You place a Stop Market Sell with a trigger of ₹262.00. It sits invisible — nobody in the market can even see it — and does nothing until the price actually touches ₹262.00. The instant it does, it fires off as a real Market order and sells at whatever price is currently available.

**4. Stop Limit** — same trigger idea as Stop Market, but once triggered, it becomes a Limit order instead of a Market order.
> Example: Same as above, but you also want to *cap* how bad a price you're willing to accept. You set a Stop Limit Sell: trigger at ₹262.00, limit at ₹261.80. Once the price hits ₹262.00, it turns into a Limit Sell at ₹261.80 — it won't sell for anything worse than that, even if the price keeps crashing further.

## Two extra "instructions" you can attach to an order

**How long should it live for? (Time in Force)**
- **Day** — cancel it automatically at the end of today if it's never filled.
- **GTC** (Good Till Cancelled) — keep it alive indefinitely, across multiple days, until you cancel it yourself.
- **IOC** (Immediate or Cancel) — fill whatever you can *right now*, and cancel whatever's left instead of letting it sit and wait.
- **GTD** (Good Till Date) — keep it alive until a specific future date you pick.

**Should it survive a hiccup? (Persistent vs. Non-Persistent)**
- **Persistent** — if your connection drops and reconnects, this order is still sitting there working.
- **Non-Persistent ("Lean")** — if your connection drops, this order automatically disappears. Useful if you're constantly re-quoting and don't want a stale, forgotten order left dangling.

**One more special instruction: Book-or-Cancel** — "Only place this order if it *doesn't* immediately match against something already there. If it would, cancel it instead of trading."
> Example: You place a Book-or-Cancel Buy at ₹263.50, but there's already a seller willing to sell at ₹263.50 right now. Instead of trading with them immediately, your order gets cancelled outright. This is for people who specifically want to sit and wait in line, never jump the queue and trade instantly.

## What we don't have in the backtester

Out of everything above, **our system only supports Limit, Market To Limit, IOC, and Book-or-Cancel.** The pieces we're missing:

- ❌ **Stop Market** and **Stop Limit** — the two "wait invisibly until triggered" order types. This is the big one: it means a strategy can't place a real stop-loss/target *at the exchange* — it has to watch the price itself and react a moment late instead (exactly the workaround `naturalgas_bracket` uses).
- ❌ **GTC** and **GTD** — orders can only last for the current day (or less); nothing that survives across multiple days.
- ❌ **Persistent vs. Non-Persistent** — every order behaves the same regardless of a connection drop; there's no "auto-cancel on disconnect" behavior modeled.
- ❌ **Auction Buy In / Sell Out** — special orders only usable during the opening/closing auction window, which this system doesn't model trading during anyway, so this one's not really a practical gap.

The Stop Market/Stop Limit gap is the one most worth caring about for strategy design, since it's the direct reason every bracket-style strategy we've built has to poll the book and react, instead of placing a real protective order and walking away.

## CLAUDE
Good question — the confusion makes total sense, and there's a clean way to see the difference. The trigger part **is** identical for both. What differs is what kind of order gets created *the instant after* the trigger fires.

## First, re-grounding Market vs. Limit (no trigger involved yet)

- **Market** = "Get me in/out right now, whatever the price is." No price control. You will almost certainly get filled, but you don't know exactly what price you'll get.
- **Limit** = "Only trade at this price or better." Full price control, but no guarantee — if the market never reaches your price, you just don't trade at all.

That's the whole tradeoff: **Market trades certainty-of-execution for price control. Limit trades price control for certainty-of-execution.** You can only ever have one, not both.

## Now: Stop Market and Stop Limit are just "wait, then become one of the above"

Both sit invisibly and do nothing until the trigger price is touched. The trigger is identical. The difference is purely: once triggered, does it turn into a **Market** order or a **Limit** order?

- **Stop Market** = trigger, then → becomes a plain Market order.
- **Stop Limit** = trigger, then → becomes a plain Limit order (at a price *you* also specify up front).

## Where it actually matters: a fast-moving market

Say you're holding Natural Gas bought at ₹263.50, and you set a protective stop at ₹262.00 because you don't want to lose more than that. Then bad news hits and the price starts crashing hard.

**With Stop Market** (trigger ₹262.00): The instant price touches ₹262.00, it fires as "sell right now, whatever price." But the market is crashing *fast* — by the time your order actually executes, the real available price might already be ₹260.50. **You definitely get out — but possibly at a much worse price than you expected.** Guaranteed execution, price is a gamble.

**With Stop Limit** (trigger ₹262.00, limit ₹261.80): The instant price touches ₹262.00, it fires as "sell, but never for less than ₹261.80." If the crash is so fast that the price blows straight through ₹261.80 before your order can fill, **your order just sits there unfilled** — nobody's buying at ₹261.80 anymore. You're protected from a terrible price, but now you might still be holding the position, and it keeps falling. **Price is protected, execution is a gamble.**

So it's the exact same tradeoff as plain Market vs. Limit — the "Stop" part just adds "and don't even show up in the market until this price is reached." Neither one is strictly better; it depends on whether you're more afraid of "getting a bad price" or "not getting out at all."

Here's what I'd have it do, in sequence, on NATURALGAS:

1. **Resting Limit** — place a Limit buy *below* the current bid (won't fill). You'll see `Submitted → Accepted` (resting), proving an order can sit in the book untouched.
2. **Cancel it** — cancel that same resting order a moment later. You'll see `PendingCancel → Canceled`, proving the cancel round-trip works.
3. **Book-or-Cancel** — place a Book-or-Cancel buy *at* the current best ask (a price that would immediately cross). You'll see it get rejected outright instead of filling — proving the "never trade, only rest" guarantee actually holds.
4. **IOC** — place an IOC buy at the best ask. You'll see whatever's immediately available fill, and anything left over auto-cancel instead of resting — proving the "fill now or forget it" behavior.
5. **Market-To-Limit** — place one of these as a real aggressive buy. You'll see a real fill (`Submitted → Filled`), a real portfolio/P&L update, and if there's a leftover unfilled amount, watch it rest instead of vanishing.

**1. Build it** (once, or after any code change):

Confirmed, with one correction to your mental model. Let me give you the precise picture.

## Who assigns `client_order_id` today

**`ExecutionEngine`** — a component that lives entirely inside qtrade, not the simulator. Found it exactly: `execution.rs` line 1198, `let client_order_id = self.clord.next();`, where `clord` is a small counter (`ClOrdIdGen`) `ExecutionEngine` owns. It fires the instant a strategy calls `ctx.submit()` — **before the order ever reaches the simulator.**

## The correction: the simulator doesn't generate a separate ID at all right now

I checked `simulator.rs` — there's no `exchange_order_id`/`venue_order_id` concept anywhere in it. `SimExchange` just reuses the **same** `client_order_id` `ExecutionEngine` already handed it as its own internal key for tracking the resting order. So today, there's only **one** ID in the whole pipeline — nothing to map, because there's nothing separate to map to.

## But real MCX genuinely does have both — and it maps almost exactly onto what you described

I checked the real MCX ETI spec, and it confirms your instinct precisely:

- **`ClOrdID` (tag 11)**: *"Client Order ID: Unique **participant**-defined order request identifier."* This is exactly `client_order_id` — **we** (the trading firm) generate it and send it *to* the exchange.
- **`OrderID` (tag 37)**: *"Exchange Order ID generated by the MCX System; it remains constant."* This is the real exchange-assigned ID, generated by MCX, sent back to us in the Execution Report.

So your mental model is right for real MCX — there genuinely are two IDs, and `ExecutionEngine` (or its future live counterpart) would be the natural place to map between them.

## One thing worth flagging, since it changes "I don't think it's needed"

I checked §4.6/4.7 of the real spec (Cancellation/Modification), and it says: *"The participant should specify the **OrderID (37)** and instrument identifier to identify the corresponding order to cancel/modify."* — **not** `ClOrdID`. So a real, live cancel/modify request has to reference MCX's own exchange-assigned `OrderID`, not our `ClOrdID` alone. That means when a real "Exchange Gateway" eventually gets built (the live counterpart to `SimExchange`, still not built), it **would** need to keep an internal `client_order_id → OrderID` mapping — otherwise it couldn't correctly cancel or modify a live order at all.

The good news: this mapping stays entirely inside the gateway. The strategy itself — everything `Ctx` exposes — only ever deals with `client_order_id`, exactly as you assumed. It's just that "I don't think it's needed" isn't quite right; it's needed *somewhere*, just never surfaced up to strategy code.

## CLAUDE
My opinion: **yes, this is the right design, and it's not speculative — it's needed to correctly model something we just confirmed from the real spec.** A few things worth being precise about before deciding whether to build it now.

## Your proposal matches an invariant this project already committed to

`ARCHITECTURE.md` §4.12 already states, before any of us touched this code: *"[`ExecutionEngine`] cannot tell the Simulated Exchange from the Exchange Gateway. Both present the same interface: commands in, reports out."* Your proposal — `ExecutionEngine` owns the `client_order_id ↔ OrderID` mapping, the venue only ever sees `OrderID`, and this works identically whether the venue is `SimExchange` or a real future live gateway — is exactly what that invariant is asking for. It's the same principle already applied to one more boundary.

## This isn't just tidiness — it's a real correctness gap for live

We just confirmed §4.6/4.7 of the real spec: cancel and modify on real MCX require **`OrderID (37)`**, not `ClOrdID`. If a future live gateway tried to pass our `client_order_id` straight through to a real MCX cancel request, it would be **wrong** — not just inelegant. So this mapping has to exist *somewhere* for live to ever work; the only real question is whether we build the muscle for it now, in the backtest, where it's cheap and testable, or discover it's missing later when live actually gets built.

## The one real implementation wrinkle

Today, `SimExchange`'s entire public interface (`submit`, `cancel`, `modify`) is keyed directly on `client_order_id` — its internal order-slot storage doesn't know any other identity exists. Making this real means:
- `SimExchange::submit` generates and returns its own order id (standing in for MCX's real `OrderID`) alongside its usual response.
- `SimExchange::cancel`/`modify` take *that* id, not `client_order_id`.
- `ExecutionEngine` keeps the `client_order_id → OrderID` table, translating on every venue call — exactly your "swap it right before talking to the venue" idea.

That's a real, mechanical change across `simulator.rs` and `execution.rs` — contained, but not a five-minute tweak, and it touches enough existing tests that they'd need updating too.

## Worth flagging honestly

One thing that makes this a bit different from most of what `SimExchange` already validates: everything else in the simulator gets checked against *real recorded MCX behavior* (real trade volumes, real book snapshots — recall D31's four-layer validation). A simulated `OrderID` has nothing real to validate against, since we don't have a real capture of MCX's own execution-report `OrderID` values — it's necessarily a stand-in, not something we can prove "matches reality" the way queue position or fill price can be checked.

**My recommendation**: build it. It's real, it's small, and doing it now means the future live cutover needs zero changes to `ExecutionEngine`'s interface — provably, not just by assumption. This is the kind of thing that belongs as a proper recorded decision (the way D12, D13, etc. are), given it changes a public interface. Want me to draft that as a decision first, or just go build it directly?

```rust
    pub venue_order_id: Option<u64>,  // new
    ...
}
```

This answers: *"given a `client_order_id` a strategy just gave me (via `ctx.cancel(id)`), what venue-side id do I actually send downstream?"* One field per order, no separate hashmap needed — it's just sitting on the order record `ExecutionEngine` already keeps in `self.orders: HashMap<u64, Order>`.

## Mapping 2: `SimExchange` — "whose order is this?"

This is the one your question is really about. When `ExecutionEngine` calls `venue.cancel(venue_order_id, now_ns)`, `SimExchange` receives a `venue_order_id` it's never seen used as a key before — its own internal bookkeeping (`resting: HashMap<client_order_id, RestingSimOrder>`) is still keyed by `client_order_id`, because several *other* existing methods (`resting_qty_ahead`, `resting_price` — both called by strategies via `Ctx`, using `client_order_id`) need that keying to stay exactly as-is.

So `SimExchange` needs its own small reverse-index to bridge the two: `resting_by_venue_order_id: HashMap<venue_order_id, client_order_id>`, letting it translate an incoming `venue_order_id` back to its own `client_order_id`-keyed storage in one lookup, then proceed exactly as it does today. **This lives on `SimExchange`, saved as one of its own struct fields** — right alongside the existing `resting_by_sim: HashMap<sim_id, client_order_id>`, which already does this exact same job for the *other* secondary key (`sim_id`) already in this file. It's not a new idiom — it's the same pattern the file already uses, just applied a second time.

To be concrete about why both are needed and neither is redundant: `ExecutionEngine`'s field answers "what do I send," `SimExchange`'s map answers "what do I do with what I received" — they're on opposite sides of the same call, so collapsing them into one wouldn't actually work; each side only ever sees its own half of the exchange.

## CLAUDE
Here's the actual flow now, step by step, with concrete numbers.

## Before the change

A strategy calls `ctx.submit(...)`. `ExecutionEngine` assigns `client_order_id` (say `1099511627776`) and sends that **same number** straight to `SimExchange` for everything — submit, cancel, modify. One id, used everywhere.

## After the change

**1. Submit** — unchanged: `ExecutionEngine` still assigns `client_order_id = 1099511627776` the instant `ctx.submit()` is called, before the venue sees anything.

**2. The order reaches `SimExchange`.** If it's accepted (rests, fills, or both), `SimExchange` now *also* mints a brand-new `venue_order_id` from its own separate counter — say `0`, since it's the first order this run. It sends this back to `ExecutionEngine` bundled into the same report (`ExecReport::Resting` or `ExecReport::Filled`), alongside the `client_order_id` it already knew.

**3. `ExecutionEngine` learns the mapping for the first time.** The moment that report comes back, it stores `venue_order_id = Some(0)` on its own record for order `1099511627776`. Before this report arrives, that field is `None` — there's nothing to map yet, since the venue hasn't accepted anything.

**4. Later, the strategy wants to cancel or modify.** It still only ever calls `ctx.cancel(1099511627776)` — the strategy never sees or touches `venue_order_id` at all, exactly as before. But now, instead of forwarding `1099511627776` straight to the venue, `ExecutionEngine` looks up what it stored in step 3, finds `venue_order_id = 0`, and sends **`0`** to `SimExchange::cancel`/`modify` — not the client id.

**5. `SimExchange` translates it back.** It receives `0`, looks it up in its own new reverse-index (`0 → 1099511627776`), and from there proceeds with exactly the same cancel/modify logic it always had — just reached via one extra translation step.

## The one behavior this is designed to prove

If that order gets **modified** (say, re-priced), `venue_order_id` stays `0` — it never changes for the life of the order, matching real MCX's `OrderID` ("remains constant"). This is different from the pre-existing `sim_id` (an unrelated internal priority-tracking number), which genuinely does get a fresh value on a price-changing modify, because real queue priority is lost. I wrote a test specifically checking this: same `venue_order_id` before and after a modify, but a *different* `sim_id` — proving the two ids behave independently, the way the real exchange's `OrderID` vs. queue position do.

**Net effect for you right now**: nothing looks different in any log, because none of this reached logging — it's a pure internal correctness fix so that a future live connection to real MCX would send the exchange's own `OrderID` on cancel/modify (which real MCX requires) instead of our own `ClOrdID` (which real MCX would reject for that purpose).

now what is this sim_id ?

## CLAUDE
Totally fair to be confused — now there are three numbers floating around. Let me isolate just `sim_id` and explain why it exists at all, since it's actually doing a completely different job than the other two.

## The other two are about *identity* — `sim_id` is about *position in line*

- `client_order_id` = the number **we** write on our own order slip.
- `venue_order_id` = the receipt number **the exchange** hands back when it accepts our order.
- `sim_id` = **our literal spot in the queue** — like a numbered ticket at a deli counter. "You are person #9,000,000,000,000,000,047 in this line."

## Why does the simulator even need a "spot in line" number?

Remember: real MCX doesn't broadcast order IDs for the public order book — it only tells everyone "here's the order that arrived at this exact timestamp." That timestamp *is* how priority in the queue is decided — whoever arrived earlier sits closer to the front.

So when our own book-building code needs to slot **our own** resting order into that same queue (to answer "how much quantity is sitting ahead of me?"), it needs something shaped like one of those arrival timestamps to sort by. `sim_id` is exactly that — a fake, made-up "arrival timestamp" for our own orders, deliberately picked from a huge, weird number range (starting around 9 quintillion) specifically so it can *never* accidentally collide with a real arrival timestamp from the actual market data. It's pure internal plumbing for the queue data structure — it isn't modeling any real MCX protocol field at all, unlike the other two.

## Why does *this one* reset on a modify, when `venue_order_id` doesn't?

Because this is exactly what queue position is supposed to do. If you change your order's price, real MCX genuinely sends you to the **back of a different line** — you lose your old spot. Since `sim_id` literally represents "your spot in line," it *has* to get a new value when you're placed in a new line. But your receipt number (`venue_order_id`) doesn't change just because you moved lines — it's still the same order, the exchange just repositioned it.

That's also exactly why I wrote that regression test: submit an order, modify its price, and check — `venue_order_id` stays the same (same receipt), but `sim_id`/`priority_ts` changes (new spot in a new line). Two numbers, two completely different jobs, both changing (or not changing) for good reason.


`main.rs` builds everything, then calls the strategy's `on_start`. The strategy asks "what's NATURALGAS's real token today?", gets `561496` from the day's contract file, and registers itself as subscriber #0 for top-of-book updates. Timestamps read `--` because no market data has been replayed yet — there is genuinely no simulated clock value to print. Then it goes quiet and waits.

## Phase 1 — Replay begins (line 4)

```
10:05:02.453  SCRIPT: starting -- NATURALGAS bid Rs 263.20 / ask Rs 263.40, tick Rs 0.10
```

The engine has been chewing through real capture data since the session's start, feeding the book. This is the first tick at-or-after the strategy's armed time of 10:05, so `run_script` wakes up, reads the live book (bid ₹263.20 / ask ₹263.40) and the real tick size (₹0.10) from reference data, and arms step 1. From here, each step fires on the first real market tick ~20 seconds after the previous one — that's why the gaps are 20.1s, 21.5s, 23.8s and so on rather than exactly 20.000s. The strategy has no timer; it's polling the clock on every tick.

## Step 1 — `Denied`: killed inside qtrade, never reached the venue (lines 5-8)

```
10:05:23.915  STEP 1/8 DENIED: submit BUY 1100 lots (over freeze) LimitDay @ Rs 261.20
10:05:23.915  [ExecutionEngine] Denied: client_order_id=1099511627776 venue_order_id=NA denied: FREEZE_QTY
10:05:23.915  [ControlDispatcher] DISPATCH: on_order_update(...state=Denied)
10:05:23.915  [OrderLifecycleDemo] ORDER_UPDATE: ...state=Denied -- denied: FREEZE_QTY
```

The strategy deliberately asks for 1,100 lots — over MCX's real freeze quantity for this contract. `ExecutionEngine` assigns `client_order_id=1099511627776` (this is `2^40`, i.e. session 1, counter 0 — the first order of the run), runs its local gates, and the freeze-quantity gate rejects it.

**Look at the timestamps: all four lines are at the identical nanosecond.** That's the tell — this order never travelled anywhere. It died inside qtrade. `venue_order_id=NA` says the same thing structurally: the venue never saw it, so it never assigned an identity.

## Step 2 — `Rejected`: reached the venue, refused there (lines 9-15)

```
10:05:44.257313039  Submitted:  ...1099511627777 venue_order_id=NA
10:05:44.257813039  Rejected:   ...1099511627777 venue_order_id=NA  venue rejected: WouldCross
```

A Book-or-Cancel buy priced right at the ask (₹263.40). BOC is post-only — it must rest, never trade — and at the ask it would immediately cross, so the venue refuses it.

**Now compare timestamps: `257313039` → `257813039` = exactly 500,000 ns.** That's the configured order latency, 250µs out + 250µs back. This order genuinely made the round trip to `SimExchange` and came back refused — visibly different from step 1's zero-gap local death. Still `NA`, because a rejected order never entered the book.

## Step 3 — `Accepted`: the first order to get a venue identity (lines 16-23)

```
10:06:08.100472974  Submitted: ...1099511627778 venue_order_id=NA
10:06:08.100972974  Accepted:  ...1099511627778 venue_order_id=0   resting
```

A limit buy at ₹261.70 — deliberately deep below the ₹263.20 bid so it cannot fill. Same 500µs round trip, and this time the venue accepts it and it rests in the book. **This is the moment `venue_order_id=0` is born** — the venue's own identity for this order, the first one it ever assigned this run.

## Step 4 — `PendingUpdate` → `Accepted`: the modify (lines 24-30)

```
10:06:29.833718452  PendingUpdate: ...1099511627778 venue_order_id=0  modify requested
10:06:29.834218452  Accepted:      ...1099511627778 venue_order_id=0  resting
```

Re-price that resting order from ₹261.70 to ₹262.40. Note the two-phase shape: `PendingUpdate` is recorded locally the instant we ask, then 500µs later the venue confirms it's working again at the new price.

**`venue_order_id` stays `0` on both lines.** This is the property the whole identity change exists to guarantee — same order, same venue identity, even though internally its queue priority was destroyed and it went to the back of the new price level's line.

## Step 5 — `PendingCancel` → `Canceled` (lines 31-37)

```
10:06:49.961719895  PendingCancel: ...1099511627778 venue_order_id=0  cancel requested
10:06:49.962219895  Canceled:      ...1099511627778 venue_order_id=0  canceled: Explicit
```

Same two-phase pattern, same 500µs. And this is where the new identity does real work: `ExecutionEngine` looked up that stored `venue_order_id=0` and sent **that** to the venue, not the client id — exactly as real MCX requires for a cancel. Order 1099511627778's life is now complete: submitted → accepted → modified → cancelled.

## Step 6 — `PartiallyFilled`: one order, two outcomes at once (lines 38-50)

```
10:07:12.505738366  Submitted:       ...1099511627779 venue_order_id=NA
10:07:12.506238366  PartiallyFilled: ...1099511627779 venue_order_id=1  partially filled qty=810000 (leaves=8190000)
10:07:12.506238366  PartiallyFilled: ...1099511627779 venue_order_id=1  remainder working after partial fill
10:07:12.506238366  [ControlDispatcher] DISPATCH: on_fill(...price=26340000000 qty=810000)
10:07:12.506238366  [OrderLifecycleDemo] FILL: ...side=Buy price=Rs 263.40 qty=81 lots
```

A 900-lot buy priced right at the ask. Only ~81 lots were actually resting there, so it swept those and the remaining 819 lots rested as a new bid. That's why you see **two** state lines from a single order: one for the fill, one for the working remainder. `venue_order_id=1` — the second order the venue accepted — and it's the same on both, since it's one order doing two things.

The strategy learns about it through two different callbacks: `on_fill` (the trade itself, with real price and quantity) and `on_order_update` (the state change). That's the deliberate split — fills and state transitions are separate channels.

## Step 7 — cancelling a partially-filled order (lines 51-57)

```
10:07:33.438949161  PendingCancel: ...1099511627779 venue_order_id=1
10:07:33.439449161  Canceled:      ...1099511627779 venue_order_id=1  canceled: Explicit
```

Pulls the 819-lot remainder. Proves cancel works from `PartiallyFilled`, not just from a clean `Accepted` — and that the 81 lots already bought stay bought (they show up as inventory in the final report).

## Step 8 — `Filled`: straight through, no resting (lines 58-67)

```
10:07:53.871695315  Submitted: ...1099511627780 venue_order_id=NA
10:07:53.872195315  Filled:    ...1099511627780 venue_order_id=2   filled qty=10000 kind=Aggressive
                    FILL: side=Sell price=Rs 263.20 qty=1 lots
```

A market-to-limit sell of 1 lot — hits the bid at ₹263.20 and fills instantly. Note there's **no `Accepted` line at all**: it never rested, it went `Submitted → Filled` directly. `venue_order_id=2`, the third and final accepted order.

## The shape that repeats every single time

Every order follows the identical path, and you can see all four participants in the log:

```
OrderLifecycleDemo  →  ExecutionEngine  →  [SimExchange]  →  ControlDispatcher  →  OrderLifecycleDemo
   (decides)            (gates, IDs,       (matches, 500µs     (routes answer      (learns via
                         accounting)        round trip)         back)               on_fill/on_order_update)
```

`SimExchange` never writes its own log lines — you infer it entirely from the 500µs timestamp gap and the state change that comes back. And the strategy never talks to it directly; every message goes out through `ExecutionEngine` and comes back through `ControlDispatcher`.

**Final tally:** 5 submit attempts → 1 died locally (`Denied`), 1 refused at the venue (`Rejected`), 3 genuinely accepted (venue ids `0`, `1`, `2`) → of those, 2 cancelled and 1 filled outright, with 81 lots bought along the way that were never sold, which is why the run ends holding inventory and showing a cost-driven negative P&L.
